key_terms.meaning: Height of the waveform from its centre line; measured in volts (or amperes, or watts of light power).
Number of full cycles the wave completes in one second; measured in hertz (Hz), f = 1/T where T is the period in seconds.
Position of the wave relative to a fixed starting point, measured in degrees or radians; one full cycle is 360° or 2π.
Loss of signal strength with distance, measured in decibels: dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁).
Change of a signal's shape because different frequency components travel at different speeds and arrive at different times.
Unwanted electrical energy added to the signal by heat, crosstalk, motors or lightning; measured as a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
Ceiling for a noiseless channel: bit rate = 2 × B × log₂ L bits per second, where B is bandwidth in Hz and L is the number of signal levels.
Ceiling for a noisy channel: C = B × log₂(1 + SNR) bits per second, with SNR as a plain ratio, not in dB.
Media that confine the signal to a solid path: twisted pair, coaxial cable and optical fibre.
Media that carry the signal through air, vacuum or water: radio, microwave, infrared and satellite links.
Rule that converts a bit stream into a voltage or light-level pattern on the link, e.g. NRZ-L, NRZ-I, Manchester.
Line code in which every bit has a transition in the middle of the bit interval; a high-to-low middle transition means 1, low-to-high means 0.
A high-frequency sine wave used as a vehicle; modulation changes its amplitude, frequency or phase to carry the data.
Quadrature amplitude modulation: combines amplitude and phase shifts on two carriers 90° apart, giving 2ⁿ points for n bits per symbol.
Frequency-division multiplexing: each signal gets its own slice of the link's frequency band, with guard bands in between.
Unused strip of frequency (or time) between neighbouring channels that stops them from interfering.
Time-division multiplexing where every source gets a fixed, repeating time slot, whether or not it has data to send.
Wavelength-division multiplexing with many closely spaced light wavelengths on one fibre, typically dozens of channels.
Direct-sequence spread spectrum: each data bit is multiplied by a fast chip code, spreading the energy over a wide band.
Improvement from spreading, in dB: 10 log₁₀(chip rate ÷ bit rate).

takeaways: A sine wave is fully described by amplitude, frequency and phase; change any one of them and you can carry information.
Attenuation, distortion and noise are three separate faults: one loses strength, one smears shape, one adds foreign energy.
Nyquist gives the level-limited ceiling on a clean channel; Shannon gives the noise-limited ceiling on a real one; the usable rate is the lower of the two.
Twisted pair is cheap and adequate to a few hundred metres, coax lasts longer at higher frequency, fibre wins on bandwidth and distance, wireless wins on mobility.
A good line code keeps the average voltage near zero (no DC drift) and creates frequent transitions so the receiver clock stays locked.
Modulation shifts a baseband signal into a band-pass channel; ASK, FSK, PSK and QAM are the digital versions of AM, FM and PM.
Multiplexing raises the utilisation of an expensive link: FDM and WDM share frequency, TDM shares time.
Spread spectrum trades bandwidth for robustness and privacy, so it survives jamming and hides below the noise floor.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always ask you to draw a waveform or spectrum, compute a Nyquist/Shannon or multiplexing number, and then compare two schemes on bandwidth, noise immunity and cost.

bank.q: Explain amplitude, frequency and phase with reference to a periodic analog signal. Draw how a change in each one alters the waveform.
outline: Define period T and frequency f = 1/T, with units Hz
Amplitude in volts measured from the centre line
Phase in degrees/radians; 360° = one cycle
Three sketches: taller wave, compressed wave, shifted wave

bank.q: Distinguish between attenuation, distortion and noise. Give one physical cause and one remedy for each.
outline: Attenuation = loss of power with distance, dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁); remedy: amplifiers and repeaters
Distortion = different propagation speeds of different frequencies, smears the shape; remedy: equalisation
Noise = thermal, induced, crosstalk, impulse; remedy: shielding, twisted pairs, higher SNR
Point out that all three act at once and are measured separately

bank.q: Compare twisted pair, coaxial cable, optical fibre and wireless as transmission media, giving one typical application for each.
outline: Construction of each medium
Bandwidth, attenuation and distance limits
Immunity to electromagnetic interference
Cost and installation ease
Applications: LAN, cable TV, backbone and FTTH, mobile/Wi-Fi

bank.q: Explain FDM, synchronous TDM and statistical TDM. State one practical system where each is used.
outline: FDM: band split, guard bands, analog or analog-like use
Synchronous TDM: fixed interleaved slots, wasted slots when a source is idle
Statistical TDM: slots given on demand, addresses needed, buffers and delay
Synchronous versus asynchronous comparison table

bank.q: A channel has a bandwidth of 3 kHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 30 dB. Find the Shannon capacity. What Nyquist bit rate is possible if 4 signal levels are used, and what does the comparison tell you?
outline: Convert 30 dB to a ratio: SNR = 10^(30/10) = 1000
Nyquist = 2 × 3000 × log₂ 4 = 12 kbps
Nyquist alone ignores noise; the real limit is the smaller or noise-adjusted figure

bank.q: Encode the bit stream 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 using NRZ-L, NRZ-I, Manchester and differential Manchester. State which schemes have a DC component and which are self-clocking.
outline: Correct waveform for each scheme with voltage levels labelled
NRZ-L and NRZ-I have DC and long runs with no transition
Manchester and differential Manchester always transition mid-bit, so they are self-clocking
Manchester needs twice the bandwidth of NRZ

bank.q: Eight sources, each producing 1000 characters per second, are multiplexed by synchronous TDM. Each character is 8 bits and one framing bit is added per frame. Find the output bit rate.
outline: Each source contributes 8000 bps
Eight sources give 64,000 bps of data
Frame carries 8 × 8 = 64 data bits plus 1 framing bit = 65 bits
Frames per second = 1000, so line rate = 65,000 bps
Comment on the overhead percentage

bank.q: A 16-QAM system runs at a baud rate of 2400 symbols per second on a channel. Find the bit rate and state the minimum bandwidth needed.
outline: 16-QAM carries log₂16 = 4 bits per symbol
Bit rate = 2400 × 4 = 9600 bps
For QAM the bandwidth is approximately the baud rate, so about 2400 Hz
Trade-off: more points give more bits but need a better SNR

bank.q: A signal of 100 mW enters a cable and 1 mW leaves at the far end. Find the loss in decibels. If the cable loses 3 dB per kilometre, how long is it?
outline: dB = 10 log₁₀(1/100) = −20 dB, i.e. a loss of 20 dB
Length = 20 ÷ 3 ≈ 6.7 km
Explain that dB is additive over cascaded links
Note that repeaters or amplifiers restore the level

bank.q: Two campuses 5 km apart must be linked at 1 Gbps through an area with heavy electrical interference. Compare twisted pair, coaxial cable, optical fibre and a microwave link on bandwidth, attenuation, noise immunity and cost, and recommend one.
outline: Twisted pair: cheap but limited to hundreds of metres at 1 Gbps, poor interference immunity
Coax: better bandwidth and shielding but still attenuates at high bit rates over 5 km
Fibre: huge bandwidth, very low attenuation, immune to electromagnetic interference, cost of termination
Microwave: no cable but needs line of sight and a licence, affected by rain
Justified recommendation with repeaters/regenerators counted

bank.q: You must design a link that carries 10 Mbps over a noisy 1 MHz channel. Choose a line code, a modulation scheme and a multiplexing method, justifying each choice with bandwidth and noise arguments.
outline: Shannon limit for the given bandwidth and SNR
Need multi-level signalling: QAM or multi-level line code
Line code chosen for clock recovery and low DC (e.g. Manchester for short links, 4B/5B or 8B/10B for efficiency)
Self-synchronisation and scrambling for long runs of identical bits
Multiplexing chosen on traffic pattern: synchronous TDM for fixed streams, statistical TDM for bursty data
Mention equalisation and error detection

bank.q: Compare direct-sequence and frequency-hopping spread spectrum with FDM. Explain how each handles interference, and say which suits a military link and which suits a Wi-Fi LAN.
outline: DSSS: chip code multiplies each bit, wideband signal, processing gain
FHSS: carrier hops over frequencies on a pseudorandom schedule
FDM: separate bands, no spreading, vulnerable to a narrow jammer
Spreading hides the signal below noise and resists jamming; FDM is simple and efficient for many steady channels
Recommendation with reasons

bank.q: Nyquist's formula gives a bit rate for a noiseless channel. Explain why using it alone on a real channel misleads a designer, and how equalisation and coding help reach the Shannon limit.
outline: Nyquist depends only on bandwidth and levels; noise is assumed zero
Real channels have SNR; more levels mean closer constellation points and more errors
Shannon gives the ceiling; the design target is just below it
Equalisation flattens the channel response and reduces distortion
Coding and trellis modulation approach capacity; interleaving handles burst errors

glossary.def: A changing physical quantity such as voltage or light intensity that carries information from one point to another.
A signal that can take any value in a continuous range and changes smoothly with time.
A signal that holds one of a fixed set of levels, changing in steps rather than smoothly.
Time taken by one complete cycle of a periodic signal, measured in seconds.
Width of the range of frequencies a signal occupies or a channel can carry, measured in hertz.
Number of bits transmitted per second, measured in bits per second (bps).
Number of signal symbols or level changes per second; for multi-level schemes the bit rate is higher.
Logarithmic unit for power ratio: dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁); a negative value means loss.
Signal-to-noise ratio, the signal power divided by the noise power at the same point, a plain ratio.
Circuit or filter that compensates for the different attenuation and delay of different frequencies on a link.
Device that regenerates a digital signal, restoring its levels and shape before sending it onward.
Device that boosts the strength of a signal, including any noise already mixed with it.
Transmission of a signal in its original frequency range, starting near zero hertz.
Device that modulates digital data onto an analog carrier and demodulates the incoming carrier back to data.
Channel that passes only a range of frequencies well above zero, so the signal must be shifted onto a carrier.
Diagram of the allowed amplitude and phase states of a modulated carrier, one point per symbol.
Extra bit added once per TDM frame to mark its boundary so the receiver can stay aligned.
Inserting an extra bit into a data stream to keep frame boundaries unambiguous, removed at the receiver.
Time-division multiplexing that assigns slots only to sources with data waiting, using addresses in each slot.
Wavelength-division multiplexing: several light wavelengths share one fibre, the optical form of FDM.
Fast pseudorandom bit sequence in DSSS that multiplies each data bit and spreads it over a wide band.
Spread-spectrum technique in which the carrier jumps among frequencies on a pseudorandom schedule.
A path that light can take inside a fibre; single-mode fibre allows one path, multimode fibre allows many.
Unwanted coupling of signal from one conductor or channel into a neighbouring one.
